part_title: EC2 Fundamentals and AI Accelerator Choices
review_basis: Visually inspected all 29 original public/course-visuals/aif-course/module-08 numbered WebP images individually in order. Narration rewritten following exact diagram arrows, visible text/examples, numeric values, callouts, and exam comparisons, with product lifecycle caveats.

scenes.title: Amazon EC2
scenes.narration: Read the deployment topology at the top. Users send web traffic to an Elastic Load Balancer, which distributes requests toward two healthy EC2 instances. Each instance has its own Amazon EBS storage, and the security group controls the allowed network traffic. An Auto Scaling group maintains the intended instance count and can replace unhealthy instances or adjust capacity according to policy. The lower example shows normal traffic with two instances; after a traffic spike an Auto Scaling group adds a third instance, while the load balancer continues distributing requests. The right panel identifies the jobs separately: EC2 runs code, EBS supplies attached block storage, the load balancer distributes traffic, Auto Scaling manages fleet size, and the security group acts as a stateful traffic filter. The multiple-choice question asks which component increases instance count; the correct answer is the Auto Scaling group, not EC2 or the load balancer by itself.

scenes.title: EC2 sizing & configuration options
scenes.narration: The slide is a six-column EC2 configuration checklist, so follow it in numerical order. First select an operating system or compatible AMI, such as Amazon Linux or Windows Server. Second choose virtual CPU and memory for the application. Third choose storage: EBS for persistent attached block volumes, instance store for local ephemeral space, and EFS when shared file-system access is required. Fourth configure the network interface, private address and optional public connectivity within a VPC subnet. Fifth restrict the security group's inbound and outbound rules, such as permitting HTTPS on port 443 for a web API. Sixth supply user data to install or configure the application at startup, without embedding secrets. The lower worked example assembles exactly these choices for a small web API, including two vCPUs, four GiB RAM, EBS and port 443. The right panels reinforce persistence and user-data caveats. Remember that stopping an instance is different from terminating it, and storage retention depends on configuration.

scenes.title: AWS hardware choices for AI workloads
scenes.narration: Begin with the top architecture: a company prepares data and trains a model, stores the completed trained model, and then deploys it behind an inference API for online or batch requests. The right side points from training toward Trainium-powered Trn instances, while inference routes toward Inferentia-powered Inf instances. The lower panels compare three accelerator choices. GPU-based EC2 P and G families support compatible training and inference software, but GPU type and software support vary. Trainium, using AWS Neuron tooling, focuses on model training and may support some inference use cases. Inferentia, also using supported Neuron tooling, is optimized for serving inference. The worked example trains a large model on a compatible GPU or Trainium instance and then serves it with compatible GPU or Inferentia capacity. The final exam panel asks you to match the workload to hardware and software requirements, not to assume one chip universally wins on price or performance.
